blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews Schmidhuber's 2014 paper, 'Deep Learning in Neural Networks: An Overview,' which serves as a comprehensive survey of deep learning (DL) up to that point. The paper traces the origins of DL through decades of research, culminating in a 35-page summary with 53 pages of references—totaling around 900 works. Colyer highlights the vastness of the field and the challenge of distilling such a broad body of knowledge. The paper introduces key concepts like the 'credit assignment problem' and 'Credit Assignment Paths (CAPs),' which measure the depth of learning in neural networks (NNs). It explores themes such as dynamic programming, unsupervised learning, hierarchical representations, and the role of GPUs in accelerating NN training. The survey also covers supervised and unsupervised learning methods, reinforcement learning, and the historical development of architectures like convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and backpropagation.
paper_title: Deep Learning in Neural Networks: An Overview
paper_abstract: In recent years, deep artificial neural networks (including recurrent ones) have won numerous contests in pattern recognition and machine learning. This historical survey compactly summarises relevant work, much of it from the previous millennium. Shallow and deep learners are distinguished by the depth of their credit assignment paths, which are chains of possibly learnable, causal links between actions and effects. I review deep supervised learning (also recapitulating the history of backpropagation), unsupervised learning, reinforcement learning & evolutionary computation, and indirect search for short programs encoding deep and large networks. LATEX source: http://www.idsia.ch/˜juergen/DeepLearning8Oct2014.tex Complete BIBTEX file (888 kB): http://www.idsia.ch/˜juergen/deep.bib Preface This is the preprint of an invited Deep Learning (DL) overview. One of its goals is to assign credit to those who contributed to the present state of the art. I acknowledge the limitations of attempting to achieve this goal. The DL research community itself may be viewed as a continually evolving, deep network of scientists who have influenced each other in complex ways. Starting from recent DL results, I tried to trace back the origins of relevant ideas through the past half century and beyond, sometimes using “local search” to follow citations of citations backwards in time. Since not all DL publications properly acknowledge earlier relevant work, additional global search strategies were employed, aided by consulting numerous neural network experts. As a result, the present preprint mostly consists of references. Nevertheless, through an expert selection bias I may have missed important work. A related bias was surely introduced by my special familiarity with the work of my own DL research group in the past quarter-century.
